description: Hey! We’re Moroccan engineering students in CS and electrical hardware with a huge passion for space tech. Backed by local and international hackathon experience, we cover the full technical stack from low-level embedded systems to web UI and know how to prototype fast under tight deadlines. Excited to connect, build, and chat about all things aerospace reach out anytime!
summary:
KhettaraLens is a data-driven ecosystem restoration platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combats desertification by merging ancient Moroccan water engineering (Khettaras) with modern space intelligence and community action.

The Problem: 
The Sahara is rapidly expanding, burying arable land, drying up ancient underground water systems, and devastating local biodiversity.

The Scientific Proof:
The platform ingests 20 years of NASA satellite data (MODIS, GPM, GLDAS) and applies the Mann-Kendall statistical test to mathematically validate long-term drought trends. It also prepares to use NISAR radar data to track the physical movement of sand dunes in real-time.

The Ground Truth:
Satellite data is validated by a crowdsourcing module where local communities report real-time ecosystem changes, such as dried wells or declining flora and fauna.

The Actionable Solution:
A Botanical AI crosses NASA's statistical trends with crowdsourced alerts to recommend specific, highly resilient plant species (like Tamarix aphylla) capable of stabilizing dunes in targeted regions. This generates verified "Trend Cards" to guide NGO funding and local farming efforts.

The Ultimate Vision:
By mastering the harshest environments on Earth and learning to reverse desertification in the Sahara, KhettaraLens builds the foundational AI models needed to eventually terraform Mars.
details:
KhettaraLens – Roots in history, eyes in space

Summary

KhettaraLens helps protect the oases of Merzouga, Morocco, where ancient underground water channels called khettaras are threatened by drying soil and wind-blown sand. Using NASA satellite data, it finds the most suitable locations around the khettaras for planting, and the native plants most likely to thrive there.

The problem we set out to solve

For over 1,000 years, oasis communities in southern Morocco have survived in the Sahara thanks to khettaras: underground tunnels that carry water from the High Atlas mountains to palm groves by gravity alone, with no pumps. Today, drying soil and drifting sand are blocking the shafts that let these tunnels breathe, and less water reaches the fields. From the ground this damage is invisible, so managers cannot tell which locations around the khettaras are suitable for planting, and tree planting often fails because the species do not suit the local soil and wind.

Our solution: five connected layers

KhettaraLens works in layers, taking a location from raw satellite data to a decision on the ground, all delivered through our interactive website:

1.       NASA data layer: soil moisture, rainfall, wind and bare ground, collected from one GPS point.

2.       Trend-detective layer: removes the normal seasonal cycle and tests every trend statistically, with a clear verdict for each result.

3.       Map layer: shows hidden dryness, wind exposure and sand on top of the khettara alignments, so the invisible becomes visible.

4.       Decision layer: finds the most suitable locations near the khettaras for planting, and a plant selection engine suggests native species that fit each zone's moisture and wind.

5.       Field layer: farmers, agronomists and visitors upload geotagged photos that check the satellite picture and track recovery over the years.

What the data tells us

What is changing? The surface soil is dry most of the time and swings strongly with the seasons. It seems to be drying slowly from 2010 to 2026, though we have not yet confirmed this statistically. Wind peaks every spring, in April and May, and the amount of bare ground shifted slightly in late 2024.

Where? We focus on Merzouga and Hassilabied in the Tafilalet, in the heart of the Moroccan Sahara. Both sites follow the same regional pattern.

How much? About a quarter of the month-to-month changes in soil moisture are explained by rainfall. Spring winds average about 4.5 m/s, with the strongest gusts near 6.8 m/s.

Is it significant? Yes, for one link: when it rains, the soil gets wetter (statistically significant over 55 months, 2022–2026). The links with wind are inconclusive, because we only have 19 to 21 months of data to compare, and we report them that way, not as proof of no effect.

What it means in practice: plant right after rain, and protect the edges of khettara shafts in April and May, along the main northeast–southwest wind direction.

NASA data we used

•         Soil moisture (top 10 cm of soil): NASA GLDAS, 2010–2026.

•         Rainfall: NASA POWER, 2022–2026.

•         Wind: NASA MERRA-2, 2000–2002 and 2025–2026.

•         Bare ground (sand exposure): NASA MODIS, 2021–2026.

From one GPS point, our tool builds monthly series, removes the normal seasonal cycle, and applies standard trend tests (Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope) so that every claim comes with a clear verdict: significant, not significant, or inconclusive.

Choosing what to plant

We match the measured conditions with how six regional plants survive in the desert. Some reach deep water (umbrella thorn acacia, date palm), some conserve water (Sodom apple, remth, jujube) and one tolerates salt (tamarisk). Our proposed rule: where deep water is reachable, use deep-rooted species; where only dry surface soil is available, use water-saving species; along strong wind corridors, plant a windbreak such as tamarisk at the shaft edges. This is a team proposal that agronomists will validate in the field.

Learning from the ground

Inspired by how drivers report road conditions on Google Maps and Waze, local people can photograph a plant, a palm grove or an advancing dune and upload it with its location. These photos check the satellite data against reality and, over the years, build a visual record of vegetation growth and dune stabilisation. Our reference site is the Jorf khettara alignment (31°31'50.0"N, 4°29'54.7"W), where the shafts are visible from above.

From Merzouga to the rest of Africa

Merzouga and Hassilabied are our pilot sites, but the tool starts from any GPS coordinate. The Sahara has similar gravity-fed water tunnels (the foggaras), and oases across North Africa face the same two threats: drying soil and wind-driven sand. Only the coordinates, the local plant list and the field checks change.

A stepping stone to Mars

Earth is NASA's proving ground, and the Sahara is an interplanetary analog. Our ancestors showed that life can thrive in a harsh place by building underground networks that protect water from sun and wind. The methods we use here are a starting point for the same problems on Mars, which share three challenges with the Sahara:

1.       Hiding water underground. Khettaras nearly eliminate evaporation at 45°C and keep sandstorms out. On Mars, surface water boils off or freezes, so future missions must rely on lava tubes and shielded underground vaults. Earth's passive underground cooling is a practical model.

2.       Finding buried moisture with radar. Radar such as NISAR can see through metres of dry sand to buried water channels. On Mars, SHARAD and MARSIS map ice beneath the dust. Both rely on the same signal-processing maths to separate surface clutter from real underground signals.

3.       Tracking moving sand. Following dune migration in southeastern Morocco predicts when sand will bury shafts. On Mars, following sand ripples in Gale Crater and Nili Patera helps anticipate dust on rover solar panels. The physics of wind-blown sand holds on both planets, scaled by air density and gravity.

NISAR radar and the Mars application are our next phase. Today's results use GLDAS, MERRA-2, POWER and MODIS.

What we are honest about

•         NASA's grid cells cover tens of kilometres, so our results point to where to look first and do not replace on-site advice.

•         Our data series have different lengths, so each test only uses the months they share.

•         Bare-ground readings in a desert also reflect sand colour and season.

•         The soil drying since 2010 still needs a formal trend test.

•         The plant link is qualitative, based on six species, and the field photos are not yet part of the results.

What comes next

1.       Run the formal drying-trend test on soil moisture from 2010 to 2026.

2.       Fill the wind data gap from 2003 to 2024 and test strong-wind days against sand exposure.

3.       Compare satellite results with geotagged field photos, first at Hassilabied and then at Merzouga.

4.       After a khettara repair or planting, repeat the same tests to measure the effect.

5.       Extend the tool to other oases and to NISAR radar.

Our team

A 6-member Moroccan student team covering the full chain, from NASA data and statistics to water heritage, botany and design: Achraf Khairouni, Hatim Ourahou, Hajar Fadil, Taha Latif, Ouiam Ouatat and Douaa Badri.
